title: Expository Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha
excerpt: The Indian Tripitaka Master Kang Sengkai translated this sutra during the Cao Wei dynasty.

inline.s: The Indian Tripitaka Master Kang Sengkai translated this sutra during the Cao Wei dynasty.
The commentary was composed by the monk Huiyuan of Jingying Temple in the capital city during the Sui dynasty.

blocks.text: Expository Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha, Fascicle One

inline.s: [Commentary]

The sacred teachings, in brief, are of only two kinds: the Sravaka Pitaka and the Bodhisattva Pitaka. That which teaches the Dharma to sravakas is the Sravaka Pitaka; that which teaches the Dharma to bodhisattvas is the Bodhisattva Pitaka. Within the Sravaka Pitaka there are two: sravakas who are sravakas, and pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas. The former are persons who in the past sought the sravaka path, ever delighting to contemplate the four Noble Truths, thereby forming the nature of a sravaka; in their last body they met the Buddha, who taught them the four Truths, and they awakened to the Way. Being originally sravaka by nature and now again hearing the voice and awakening, they are called sravakas who are sravakas, that is, what the sutra calls 'for those who seek to be sravakas he spoke the four Truths.' The latter are persons who originally sought the pratyekabuddha path, ever delighting to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby forming the nature of a pratyekabuddha; in their last body they met the Buddha, who taught them the twelve links, and they awakened to the Way. Being originally pratyekabuddha by nature and having heard the voice and awakened in their last body, they are called pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas. Though the two attainments differ, both receive the Lesser Dharma and both awaken by hearing the voice in this present life; hence what is spoken to these two is the Sravaka Pitaka. Within the Bodhisattva Pitaka there are the gradual and the sudden. The gradual entrant studied the Great in the past, in the meanwhile practiced the Lesser and realized its fruit, and later returned to the Great, coming from the Lesser; hence 'gradual.' The sutra says, 'Except those who formerly studied the Lesser Vehicle, I shall also cause them to enter this Dharma.' The suddenly awakened are beings who have long cultivated good roots corresponding to the Great Vehicle, now first see the Buddha and are able to enter the Great, the Great not proceeding from the Lesser; hence 'sudden.' The sutra says, 'Or there are beings who, age after age, have always received my teaching; when first they see my body and hear my words, they at once believe and receive, entering the Tathagata's wisdom.' The gradual entrant relies on shallow stages and journeys far; the suddenly awakened understands the Great in a single leap. Though sudden and gradual differ, both receive the Great at the same time, so what is spoken to them is the Bodhisattva Pitaka. The sacred teachings, however many, do not pass beyond these two. Nagarjuna said that after the Buddha's nirvana Kasyapa and Ananda compiled the Dharma-storehouse at Rajagrha as the Sravaka Pitaka, and Manjusri and Ananda compiled the Mahayana on Iron-Circumference Mountain as the Bodhisattva Pitaka. The Bodhisattva-bhumi likewise says the Buddha spoke the sutras for sravakas and bodhisattvas practicing the way out of suffering, and the compilers gathered them into two Pitakas. The two are also called the Great and Lesser vehicles, the full and empty teachings; though the names are inverted, the meaning is not different. Now this sutra falls within the Bodhisattva Pitaka; it is the Dharma-wheel of sudden teaching for those of sharp and ripened faculties. We know it is sudden because it is precisely for ordinary beings who dread birth and death and seek right concentration, causing them to rouse the mind and be born in the Pure Land, not proceeding from the Lesser or the Great.
[Commentary]

Having distinguished the divisions, we next explain the title. 'The Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha' sets forth the particular name of the sutra. All sutras set the title first to show the Dharma they reveal; this sutra manifests the practice and attainment of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the beings he gathers and transforms, and therefore first raises that name. The various sutras take their names differently: some only from the Dharma, as the Nirvana; some only from a person, as the Trapusa and Prince sutras; some only from an event, as the Withered Tree sutra; some only from a simile, as the Great Cloud and Jewelled Casket sutras; some from the time, as the sutra on right and wrong times; some from a place, as the Samgha sutra and the sutra of Gaya's Peak; some raise both person and Dharma, as the Vimalakirti and the Srimati sutras; some set forth both event and Dharma, as the Vaipulya Great Assembly sutra; some reveal both Dharma and simile, as the Avatamsaka and the Lotus sutras. Thus they are not of one pattern. This sutra is named from the person. In listing the person there are four: raising the person himself, as in Vimalakirti; raising the asker, as in Manjusri's questions; raising the person spoken of, as in the Prince sutra; raising the person to be transformed, as in the sutra of Sumati's daughter. The opening of this sutra generally raises both the speaker and the spoken of: 'the Buddha' raises the speaker, and 'Immeasurable Life' the spoken of. The occasions of preaching are five, as Nagarjuna says: the Buddha speaks himself; holy worthies speak; the gods speak; gods and immortals speak; and transformed persons speak. This sutra is spoken by the Buddha, and to set it apart from the other four the word 'Buddha' is raised. 'Buddha' is a foreign word translated 'the awakened.' 'Awakened' has two senses. First, awareness, directed at the affliction-obstacle: affliction harms, with an affair like a thief, and only sages are aware of it and are not harmed thereby; this sense is as explained in the Nirvana. Second, comprehension, directed at the wisdom-obstacle: ignorance lies asleep, its affair like sleep, and when sage-wisdom arises one awakens greatly, as one wakes from sleep. The ignorance that is its object is of two kinds: the nature-veiling ignorance that obscures the real nature, which being removed the false turns to the true, so that awakening to the real is called 'awakening'; and the unknowing within events, deluded about the characteristics of dharmas, which being removed one understands all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas. Therefore the Bodhisattva-bhumi says that in the categories of benefit-to-meaning, non-benefit-to-meaning, and neither-benefit-nor-non-benefit, he opens and awakens equally; hence he is called Buddha. Since he awakens himself and also awakens others, and the practice of awakening is fully carried out, he is called Buddha. Self-awakening sets him apart from ordinary beings, awakening others from the two vehicles, and the fully completed practice from the bodhisattvas; hence only he alone is called Buddha. Uttering with the mouth is 'speaking'; 'Immeasurable Life' is what is spoken. This sutra proclaims the practice and attainment of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the beings he gathers and transforms. 'Practice' proclaims the vows he first made and the practice he first cultivated; 'attainment' speaks of the two fruits he now attains, the Dharma-body and the Pure Land; 'gathering' means he universally draws the connected beings of the ten directions to go together to that land, so that the benefit of the Dharma-transformation is called 'the gathered.' Moreover all bodhisattvas study his practice, obtain his attainment, and share his gathering; this too is 'the gathered.' The Buddha's name is of two kinds, common and particular: 'Thus-come One, Worthy of Offerings' are the common names; 'Sakyamuni, Maitreya, Immeasurable Life' are the particular designations. Among the particular names there are many: some from the lineage, as Sakyamuni and Kasyapa; some from the body, as the Honored Body Buddha; some from the voice, as the Wonderful Sound Buddha; some from the light, as the Universal Light Buddha; some from inner virtue, some from a simile. This Buddha is named from his lifespan. The lifespan has a true and an apparent one: the true is eternally abiding, its nature the same as empty space; the apparent lifespan is not fixed, sometimes long, sometimes short. What is discussed here is the apparent. Within the apparent lifespan this Buddha's life is long, and ordinary beings and the two vehicles cannot fathom its limit; hence 'immeasurable.' That this is apparent and not true we know because the Sutra of Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta says that though the life of this Buddha is long and far-reaching it too has an end, and after his nirvana the two bodhisattvas become Buddhas in succession. 'Sutra' is the foreign word 'sutra,' translated 'thread': the sayings of sages string all dharmas as a thread strings flowers. The thread strings flowers and the sutra maintains the lifespan, their functions being similar; hence 'sutra.' By the ordinary gloss 'sutra' means 'constant': people differ in past and present, but the teachings are an enduring norm; and any one Dharma passes through antiquity and reaches the present, always existing without interruption, which is its sense of 'constant.'

From beginning to end this sutra's text has but three divisions: the preface, the main teaching, and the transmission. From the beginning to 'he replied, 'I wish to hear them'' is the preface; from 'The Buddha told Ananda, 'In the past, long ago...'' onward is the main teaching; from 'The Buddha told Maitreya, 'Those who shall hear that Buddha's name and rejoice''' onward is the transmission. Transformation must have a cause, so the preface is first set forth; since the preface has arisen, the main doctrine is next set forth; and the sages preach the Dharma for the benefit of beings and, having finished, praise its excellence, urge study, and entrust it for preservation, so third the transmission is distinguished.
[Commentary]

The preface's meaning and text, though many, have an essential meaning of only two: the initiating preface and the attesting-faith preface. About to teach, the Buddha first relies on time and place, uses supernatural power to gather the assembly, and raises the principle taught; this is 'initiating,' and as the cause of the teaching it is the initiating preface. After the Buddha finishes teaching, Ananda receives the Dharma and, about to transmit it to later ages, first says to the assembly, 'Such is the Dharma, I heard it from the Buddha,' attesting it so as to be credible; this is the attesting-faith preface. Two prefaces are established because there are two sutras: the sutra spoken by the Tathagata and the sutra transmitted by Ananda. Though the substance is one, measured by persons and times it is divided in two. The Tathagata's speech benefited that time; Ananda's transmission reaches later ages. Facing the Tathagata's sutra the initiating preface is established, and facing Ananda's transmitted sutra the attesting-faith preface is established. These two prefaces have further meanings, related elsewhere.

In the text the first words, 'Thus have I heard,' are the attesting-faith preface. From 'at one time' onward the meaning has two aspects: taken as the original event's arising, it is assigned to the initiating preface; and cited by Ananda to attest the truth, it is the attesting-faith preface. Since the meaning has both aspects, one cannot take it one-sidedly.
I have heard thus.
In the attesting-faith preface there are three gates: explaining the reason for the words 'Thus have I heard'; clarifying the purpose of establishing them; and explaining their text.
[Commentary]

As to the reason, why does every sutra's opening bear the words 'Thus have I heard'? Because the Buddha directed them to be placed. Why did he direct it? Because of Ananda's request. Why did Ananda request? Because Aniruddha instructed him. Why did Aniruddha instruct? Because he saw Ananda's mind grieved. Why was Ananda grieved? Because he saw the Tathagata about to enter parinirvana. The Buddha was about to pass away, lying with head to the north between the twin sala trees; Ananda, seeing this, wept and sobbed and could not contain himself. Aniruddha awakened him, saying, 'You are the transmitter of the Dharma; why do you not ask the Buddha about the affairs of the future world? Of what use is mere grief?' Ananda replied, 'My mind has sunk in a sea of sorrow; what is there to ask?' Aniruddha then taught him to ask four matters: after the World-Honored One's nirvana, on what do the monks rely as teacher; on what do they abide; how to dwell with ill-natured monks; and what word to set at the head of all sutras. Instructed, Ananda was somewhat awakened and asked, and the Buddha answered: they should rely on the Pratimoksa as teacher; if I were still in the world it would be no different. The Pratimoksa is the precepts the monks study. They should abide by the four foundations of mindfulness — the monk relying on the inner body to cultivate contemplation of the body, striving with diligence to remove worldly craving and love, and likewise with the outer body and the inner-outer body, and likewise with feelings, mind, and dharmas. The sutra says, 'If one abides in the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called one's own realm and one is not bound by Mara; if one abides in the five desires, that is Mara's realm and one is bound by him.' To dwell with ill-natured monks, govern them with the brahma-danda, the penalty of silence; if the mind is tamed, then speak of leaving the two extremes. At the head of all sutras set 'Thus have I heard, the Buddha dwelt in such a place,' among such an assembly, and the other six matters. Because the Buddha directed this, every sutra's opening is furnished with 'Thus have I heard.' Next, the purpose. The Buddha directed this phrase to produce faith in beings. As to 'thus,' Ananda declares that he believed and obeyed the Buddha's words, saying the Buddha's speech was 'thus' and 'so,' causing other beings to join him in faith. As to 'I have heard,' Ananda is himself an insufficient person; were he to say this Dharma was his own teaching, many would despise and slander it, but because he says it was heard from the Buddha, people all turn to faith. Faith is the first gate of entering the Dharma and the foremost in embracing it. The Avatamsaka says faith is the hand: a man with a hand, on reaching a place of treasures, takes what he wishes; a man without hands obtains nothing. Having the hand of faith, one takes the treasure of the Way at will. Therefore these words are set to produce faith. Next, the phrase itself. 'Thus' has two senses. By the Dharma: Ananda says the Buddha's words are 'thus' with respect to dharmas — speaking principle as principle, events as events, cause as cause, fruit as fruit; hence 'thus'; and words that accord with the Dharma are correct in principle, hence 'so.' By the person: Ananda says the present Sakyamuni spoke 'thus' like all the Buddhas of the past; hence 'thus.' The Nirvana sutra says, 'As the past Buddhas spoke, not changing, therefore called “Thus-come.”' To be contrary to the Buddhas' speech the words are not-so; to accord with them they are so. As to 'I have heard,' Ananda, facing future beings, declares he received the teaching. Hearing is truly with the ear, yet he says 'I': the faculties differ but are all my instruments, and the speaker is set forth. In the Dharma there is no person, yet one speaks of the subject and says 'I,' because though the Dharma has no fixed subject it is not without a provisional name, as the Nirvana says: four armies combined form an army, and though there is no fixed commander one may still say 'my army is valiant.' One may ask why Ananda, a sage who has attained the principle, uses 'I' like ordinary beings. There are three kinds of 'I': the 'I' of the view-mind, the ordinary beings who have not lost the view of self; the 'I' of the pride-mind, the trainees who though free of the view of self still have pride; and the 'I' of worldly convention, the sages beyond training whose view-impurities and pride are exhausted, who follow the worldly convention and provisionally say 'I.' Ananda, when compiling the Dharma, was beyond training, his views and pride removed, and followed the worldly convention in saying 'I'; hence he is not the same as ordinary beings. But 'I' is a provisional name of worldly truth and no-self is the supreme truth, so why not take the supreme and proclaim no-self? Because the transformation of ordinary beings requires it: if one did not say 'I,' how could one distinguish this from that and cause people to know and recognize? Hence one must say 'I'; and even the Buddhas, when transforming, often say 'I,' and the wise find nothing strange.

From 'at one time' onward, though the meaning has both aspects, facing the foregoing which is entirely the attesting-faith preface, we explain it specifically as the initiating. Within it there are three: clarifying the Buddha as the transforming master; from 'with a great assembly of monks' onward, distinguishing his retinue; and from 'at that time the World-Honored One's faculties were serene' onward, the Tathagata manifests transformation as the initiation, and Ananda makes the request.
At one time the Buddha was dwelling at Rajagrha, on Mount Grdhrakuta (Vulture Peak).
[Commentary]

'At one time' raises the Buddha's time of transformation; 'the Buddha' raises the transforming person; 'dwelling at Rajagrha' raises the place of transformation. As to 'one time,' people have various explanations, but here it means the season of transformation. Through the whole of the Buddha's lifetime the times of transformation are many, and 'one' distinguishes this from the others. The phrase abounds in the sutras: the Nirvana says, 'I at one time was at Rajagrha discussing worldly truth with the bodhisattva Maitreya'; 'I at one time was on the bank of the Ganges'; 'I at one time was in the cemetery of corpses.' 'The Buddha' is as explained before. 'Rajagrha' is a general raising by the city, so called because in ancient times many kings dwelt there. Mount Grdhrakuta is a separate designation of place: around Rajagrha there are five mountains, each with a monastery, so to distinguish it the mountain is named. It is translated 'Vulture Peak' because many spirit-immortals dwell there and vultures roost there; it is also called Vulture-Head Mountain, since many spirit-vultures live on its summit and the peak resembles a vulture's head. Within the place of roaming transformation, abiding is called 'dwelling.' The Dharma-body is equal and truly has no resting place, but the transformation is manifested in a direction, hence 'dwelling'; and to make the transforming teaching universal it must follow the transformation.
[Commentary]

In the second part, the assembly, the sravakas are first listed and then the bodhisattvas are revealed; so do the many sutras. Why? The explanation in general has four points. First, by near and far: the sravakas are mostly near the Tathagata, so after the Buddha is clarified they are listed first as near; the bodhisattvas are mostly not near the Buddha, so they are listed later. Why are the sravakas especially near? For two reasons: they have not practiced the Way long and, though they have attained the sage-fruit, in progress and deportment they always follow the Buddha's teaching, as the vinaya lays down that Aniruddha should not share lodging with women, that Svagata should not drink liquor, and that the seventeen youths should not play in the water — all arhats following the Buddha's rules; whereas the bodhisattvas, long familiar with the Dharma, do not rely on his teaching. Also, the sravakas are saved by the Buddha in this life, leaving the ordinary to become sages, and the grace being deep they always attend and serve him; the bodhisattvas, transforming beings according to conditions, are mostly not near him. Second, by deportment and form: the sravakas maintain their deportment, and their form resembles the Buddha, so the world reveres them and they are listed first; the bodhisattvas, transforming according to circumstances, have indeterminate form, as when Manjusri in a single summer dwelt in three places in retreat. Third, by the teaching: as Nagarjuna explains, the teaching is manifest or secret. According to the manifest teaching, the arhats and pratyekabuddhas, like the Buddha, have the outflows extinguished, so after the Buddha the sravakas are listed; the bodhisattvas manifest the various outflows and appear as ordinary beings, so to avoid startling people they are listed last. According to the secret teaching, the bodhisattvas' virtue is venerable and they should be first, as the Avatamsaka lists the bodhisattvas first and only in the assembly of the Jetavana Double-Gallery lists the sravakas. Fourth, by number: as the Nirvana says, the fewer are listed first and the greater later. Now, by the first two senses, the sravakas are listed first, then the bodhisattvas.
Within the sravaka assembly the text has four divisions: marking the distinction of the assembly; distinguishing its number; praising its virtue; and listing its names.
Together with a great assembly of monks.
[Commentary]

First this marks the assembly, and it is by reference to the Buddha that the assembly is made clear. Taking the body together with those others is 'together.' 'Great' is the foreign word 'maha,' translated with three senses: 'many,' as many people in the world are called a great assembly; 'surpassing,' for among those ninety-five kinds of paths this is most superior; and 'great,' for it broadly possesses elevated virtue and exceeds the recent learners. 'Bhiksu' is an Indian word translated with five senses: 'one who frightens Mara' — having left home, his roused mind is vast and causes Mara to fear, for Mara is jealous and mean, begrudging others surpassing himself, and fears that he will transform many beings out of birth and death, emptying his realm; 'alms-seeker' — having left home he stores up nothing and lives by begging; 'pure livelihood' — he seeks alms by a right livelihood apart from wrong livelihood; 'one who purely observes the precepts' — keeping the precepts purely with no transgression; and 'one who destroys evil' — by observing the precepts he leaves the fault of transgression. When there are many people it is called an assembly.
Twelve thousand people were gathered together.
[Commentary]
Second, distinguishing their number. Gathering together is called 'together.'
All the great sages, whose supernormal powers have already been attained.
[Commentary]

Third, praising their virtue. 'All the great sages' praises the eminence of the persons, raising one to imply the rest. Those whom the dull-rooted and recent learners cannot surpass are called 'great' — for high in stage, as those below from Ajnata Kaundinya onwards are all ultimate sages beyond training, and for surpassing virtue, as they are all sharp-rooted sravakas accomplishing surpassing virtue. Meeting the right is 'sage.' 'Supernormal powers already attained' praises the excellence of their virtue: what is done is spirit-wondrous, hence 'spirit'; without obstruction is 'through.' The superpowers are six: the bodily superpower, the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the extinction of outflows. These monks in the Lesser Vehicle have cultivated to the ultimate, hence 'already attained.' One may ask how Ananda, who while the Buddha lived was in the stage of study and had not attained the extinction of outflows, is included. It is because, following the many, he is praised; and though his virtue was not complete he was the requester in this assembly and must be listed, and being of the highest sharp faculties he accomplished immeasurable sublime virtues in the stage of study, hence called 'great sage,' and comprehended the superpowers ultimately, hence also 'already attained.' Above is the praise of their virtue.

Their names are: the Venerable Ajnata Kaundinya, the Venerable Proper Vow, the Venerable Proper Speech, the Venerable Great Call, the Venerable Benevolent and Wise, the Venerable Free from Defilement, the Venerable Renowned, the Venerable Good and Real, the Venerable Complete, the Venerable Bull King, the Venerable Uruvilva Kasyapa, the Venerable Gaya Kasyapa, the Venerable Nadi Kasyapa, the Venerable Mahakasyapa, the Venerable Sariputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the Venerable Kapphina, the Venerable Great Abiding, the Venerable Great Pure Will, the Venerable Maha Juna, the Venerable Full of Vows, the Venerable Free from Obstacles, the Venerable Conduit, the Venerable Firm and Subduing, the Venerable Face King, the Venerable Fruit Vehicle, the Venerable Benevolent Nature, the Venerable Joy and Bliss, the Venerable Good Coming, the Venerable Rahula, the Venerable Ananda. All such as these are the elders at the head.
[Commentary]

Fourth, listing their names. 'Their names are' is the compiler's general raising, next the individual listing. These all have virtue and are venerable, hence 'Venerable.' Ajnata Kaundinya: Kaundinya is the surname, Ajnata the given name; 'a' means 'no' and 'jna' means 'wisdom,' so having realized the no and accomplished wisdom he is called 'no-wisdom.' 'No' is the original nature of all dharmas, called the original limit, and in this original limit he knows and sees clearly, hence 'Ajnata.' Of the twelve thousand, just thirty-two are listed, and 'all such as these are the elders at the head' concludes the praise generally.

Next are listed the assemblies of bodhisattvas, within which there are four: marking the distinction of the assembly; from 'Samantabhadra and the rest' listing their names; from 'possessing immeasurable virtues and practices' onward praising their virtue; and from 'such as these, beyond recounting' onward distinguishing the total number.
Together again with the great assembly of bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle.
[Commentary]

'Again' is a word of repetition; the sravakas having been listed, the bodhisattvas are now made clear. 'Together' has the same sense as before, distinguishing the Buddha and including those others. 'Great Vehicle' names the Dharma to distinguish the persons: 'vehicle' is the function of practice, which conveys and reaches; the vehicles are three, and the other two are not its equal, hence 'great.' 'An assembly of bodhisattvas' names the persons by the Dharma; not one is called an assembly. 'Bodhisattva' is a foreign word, fully 'bodhi-sattva,' abbreviated 'bodhisattva,' translated 'a being of the Way': 'bodhi' is the Way and 'sattva' is a being, for this person inwardly seeks the Way and fully possesses its practice, and is completed by the Way. One may ask why, since the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas also seek the Way and have its practice, only this one is called a being of the Way. The worthy and the sages have names both common and particular: by the common, all are included, as the Nirvana says the stream-enterer and the rest are also called bodhisattva because they seek the wisdom of the extinction of outflows and the knowledge of no-birth, and are also called Buddha because of the common and not-common right enlightenment. But to distinguish the worthy and the sages, the beings of the Great Vehicle are specifically named 'bodhisattva,' for three reasons. By the vow-mind toward the fruit: only these beings seek the great bodhi, hence only they are called beings of the Way, as the Bodhisattva-bhumi says, 'One who with fixed determination vows bodhi alone is called bodhisattva.' By the understanding-mind toward the principle: ordinary beings cling to being and the two vehicles abide in non-being, neither according with the middle Way, whereas only the bodhisattva lets go of being and non-being and accords with it. By the practice: in entering the Buddha-Dharma there are the teaching, the meaning, and the practice. The teaching is shallow, the meaning deep, and the practice most supreme. The sravakas, of dull faculties, are named from the teaching — 'sravaka' (the hearer) means hearing the voice and awakening. The pratyekabuddha, next superior, is established by the meaning — 'pratyeka' (dependent) means awakening on the conditions. The bodhisattva, most supreme, is named from the practice, being able to accomplish the Way of benefiting self, others, and both. Hence the Bodhisattva-bhumi says the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas can save only themselves, whereas the bodhisattva saves himself and others, so his Way is supreme. Gathering together is called 'together.'

Samantabhadra bodhisattva, Manjusri (Miaode) bodhisattva, Maitreya (Cishi) bodhisattva, and so forth, all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadra-kalpa (the Worthy Age). Moreover the sixteen worthies, headed by Bhadrapala: the bodhisattva Good Reflection, the bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, the bodhisattva Emptiness and No-thing, the bodhisattva Supernatural Flower, the bodhisattva Light and Radiance, the bodhisattva Wisdom Supreme, the bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, the bodhisattva Serene Root, the bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, the bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the bodhisattva Jewel Radiance, the bodhisattva Dwelling in the Middle, the bodhisattva Regulating Conduct, the bodhisattva Liberation. All these revere the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra.
[Commentary]

Next the names are listed. First those bodhisattvas who will become Buddhas in the Bhadra-kalpa are listed, and then, under Bhadrapala and the rest, the bodhisattvas of the other kalpas. Within the Bhadra-kalpa, Samantabhadra, Manjusri, and Maitreya are listed separately. Manjusri is Wenshu; Maitreya is Cishi, his surname being compassionate, and his name is Ajita, which here means 'No-Superior.' 'And so forth' are the other bodhisattvas of the Bhadra-kalpa, and 'all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadra-kalpa' generally sums them by time. In the other kalpas, sixteen worthies are briefly raised, raising the beginning to include the rest, and 'Good Reflection and the rest' lists individually those among their equals. 'All these revere the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra' reveals what they studied, and may also be called distinguishing the lower from the higher.

Next is the praise of their virtue, within which there are two divisions: praising their twofold virtue of expedience and ultimate, and, from 'whose practice is pure' onward, praising their twofold virtue of self-benefit and benefiting others. Within the former there are three: from their own division briefly praising their virtue; from 'entering the Dharma-storehouse' onward, broadly praising their virtue in progressive advance; and from 'perfect and complete virtue, wondrous' onward, jointly concluding the praise.
Possessing the immeasurable practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, abiding in all the dharmas of virtue, roaming the ten directions, employing the skillful means of expedience.
[Commentary]

In the first brief praise, first the ultimate virtue is praised and from 'roaming' onward the expedient virtue. In the ultimate, 'possessing the immeasurable practices and vows' means the practices are complete and full — 'practice' meaning the six perfections and the four methods of gathering, 'vow' meaning the immeasurable bodhi practices and vows, as the Avatamsaka speaks. 'Abiding in all the dharmas of virtue' means the completed virtue is fully furnished and, being accomplished, never retreats. Having virtue it is accomplished, hence 'all.' 'Merit' (gong) means function, for all the practices benefit; this merit is the virtue of good practice, hence 'virtue' (de). The sutra's 'virtue and merit' has a common and a particular sense; in the common sense all practices are so, in the particular the practice of wisdom is called wisdom while the remaining precepts, giving, and so forth are called virtue; here the common is taken. The substance of virtue is called 'dharma.' In the expedient praise, 'roaming the ten directions' means the body is unobstructed, and 'employing the skillful means of expedience' means the transforming activity is skillfully appropriate, appearing variously according to the fitness of beings.
Above, their virtue was briefly praised according to their own division.

Below, their virtue is broadly praised according to the progressive advance. Within it, first the ultimate virtue is praised; from 'attaining Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds' onward, the expedient virtue is praised.
Entering the Dharma-storehouse of the Buddha, reaching in the ultimate the further shore.
[Commentary]

In the ultimate, first it says 'entering the Buddha's Dharma-storehouse'; to realize and attain is called 'entering.' 'The further shore reached in the ultimate' reveals the fruit as final; the further shore of nirvana, reached, is called 'ultimate.'
In immeasurable worlds manifesting the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment.
[Commentary]

In praising the expedient virtue, 'in immeasurable worlds manifesting the accomplishment of right enlightenment' praises it in general, and as it praises the progressive advance it raises the attainment of Buddhahood as the expedient virtue.

From 'dwelling in Tushita' below it specifically reveals it. Within it, fully treated, there should be ten marks: ascending to the Tushita heaven; coming down and entering the womb; abiding in the womb; birth; the mark of the child; the mark of taking a consort; the mark of leaving home; the mark of accomplishing the Buddha-way; the mark of turning the Dharma-wheel; and the mark of parinirvana. In the present text one is missing, the abiding in the womb, leaving nine marks.
Dwelling in the Tushita heaven, widely proclaiming the correct Dharma.
[Commentary]

In the first mark, 'dwelling in the Tushita heaven' is the body ascending to Tushita. Tushita, one name variously transmitted, is translated 'splendid abundance,' also called 'contentment' — the fourth heaven of the desire-realm. Why is he born there? As the Nirvana explains, Tushita is supreme: the upper heavens are dark and dull and the lower heavens are indulgent, while this one has neither fault; and whereas giving and precepts obtain the upper and lower heavens, giving, precepts, and concentration obtain Tushita. Though Tushita is the distracted ground of the desire-realm, this is not the concentration of the eight meditations but rather, within the mind of thought-wisdom, the practice of the mindfulness of the Buddha samadhi, so one is born there in dependence on concentration. 'Widely proclaiming the correct Dharma' is the transformation by speech. This completes the first mark.
Leaving that heavenly palace, descending his spirit into the mother's womb.
[Commentary]

This is the second mark. He leaves the bliss of the highest heaven in order to cause the beings of Jambudvipa to all receive the Buddha's grace and produce a mind of reverence, thinking, 'The Buddha left heavenly bliss to be born in Jambudvipa out of compassion for us.' One may ask why of the four kinds of birth the Tathagata especially accepts womb-birth. Because egg-birth and moisture-birth have inferior retribution and transformation-birth, though supreme, has many senses; as the Nirvana says, in brief there are eight senses: at the beginning of the kalpa beings were born by transformation and their afflictions had not yet arisen, so there was no need for the Buddha to appear; when the Buddha appears in the world beings are womb-born, so to increase the power of co-born beings he accepts womb-birth; to be born in a superior clan showing forth the supremacy of the Dharma; to be born in a royal line to rely on it for protecting the Dharma; to teach people to respect the work of father and mother; to be born in a superior clan to still people's pride; to still slander — for if the Buddha were born by transformation many would say he is an apparition and not real; to leave a body and relics for the benefit of later ages — for a transformed birth would pass away as the lightning and leave nothing; and to be the same as all the Buddhas of the three times, who by the Dharma accept womb-birth. Possessing all these senses he accepts womb-birth. This is the second, finished.
According to the other sutras and treatises, here one is missing the mark of abiding in the womb. Since this is what is lacking, the third mark is hereby concluded.

Born from the right side, taking seven steps as he walked, his light shining brilliantly, universally illuminating the ten directions, immeasurable buddha-lands quaking in six ways, he raised his voice and declared, 'I shall be in this world the supreme honored one.' Sakra and Brahma attended him, and gods and men turned to him in reverence.
[Commentary]

This is the fourth mark, birth, within which there are three: the birth-place is extraordinary; what is manifested is extraordinary; and the gods and men revere and serve. In the first, the birth-place of worldly beings is impure, foul, and lowly, and the Buddha differs from them, hence he is born from the right side — and being born from the right side is as emerging from clouds and mist, the mother's body at ease, without effort and pain. Among the manifested wonders, first the wonder of the body is made clear, and from 'raised his voice' onward the wonder of speech. The body has three: in the ten directions he takes seven steps each, showing the heroic strength of a great man and standing forth alone without fear; the body-light universally illuminates, causing people to be aware; and the earth trembles, causing Mara to crouch in fear. The six kinds of quaking, as the Sutra of Stages says, are trembling, surging, shaking, quivering, roaring, and rising: quaking like a cart shaking, surging like a spring welling up or a pot boiling, shaking downward as worldly empty things fall when shaken, quivering causing the mind to be aware so that even beings in the sky know it, and roaring being the issuing of sound. From 'raised his voice' onward is the wonder of speech, self-proclaiming his honored title and causing people to come and take refuge. Finally, the Buddha's virtue being deep, he causes Sakra and Brahma to come and attend him and men and gods to turn to him in reverence. The fourth mark is finished.
